newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Canada rules out telecom ownership change at talks.
newsitem.headline: Canada rules out telecom ownership change at talks.

text.p: Senior Canadian officials said on Wednesday that Canada was unlikely to back away from a proposal blocking majority foreign ownership of domestic telecoms firms, seen as a sticking point at talks in Geneva on a global pact.

U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang said on Monday that Washington was unhappy with the fact that non-Canadians could hold only a maximum 46.7 percent equity stake in telecommunications companies.
Canadian officials defended their stance on Wednesday but said Ottawa was considering relaxing rules on domestic satellite communications.

"We don't believe the 46.7 percent foreign ownership is any barrier to entry into Canada. If you look at the totality of our package on the table, we believe we have a very good offer," said a senior trade official.
The negotiations on a global pact to liberalise the $600 billion telecommunications market, sponsored by the World Trade Organisation, are due to be completed by a Saturday deadline.
Canadian trade officials said Canada's proposal had already offered to eliminate all remaining telecoms monopolies and liberalise services completely.

"We have no flexibility to do any further movement along these lines," one senior official said, requesting anonymity. Canadian and U.S. officials had discussed the issue at length, and expressed hopes that a deal would be clinched, he added.

Canada was instead considering relaxing a law requiring the use of Canadian satellites only for domestic Canadian satellite communications. "We're thinking about relaxing that and allowing the ability to use any satellite -- American, Mexican."

Altogether 59 governments representing more than 90 per cent of the global market have submitted offers to open their domestic telecom markets to foreign operators. Sri Lanka and Tanzania were expected to present offers by the end of the week.

U.S. negotiators are now conducting an assessment of of whether they have the "critical mass" of quality offers Washington says it needs to guarantee unfettered foreign access to is own telecoms market, the world's biggest.
The United States derailed an effort last April to reach a global pact when it backed away, saying offers from emerging economies were insufficient.

Canadian officials said they saw progress towards a deal. "The European Union believes there's a deal to be had here, Japan believes there's a deal to be had here and Canada and most other countries believe there's a deal," said one.

"A lot of countries have promised to come up with offers and further improvement is promised. Some technical clarification is also required," he said. "If we get movement on these fronts, we believe there'll be enough critical mass to cut a deal."
